title: SYSK Selects: How Hip-hop Works
summary: SYSK Selects edition (Saturday pick by Josh) rerunning the 2013 episode "How Hip Hop Works." The hosts trace hip hop as a cultural movement distinct from rap, covering its four pillars (DJing, MCing/rapping, graffiti, breakdancing/dance) plus style/fashion. Topics include the African griot tradition, Caribbean/Jamaican sound system culture and toasting, dub, DJ Kool Herc's block parties and break beats, Cookie Rock and Clark Kent as early rappers, Afrika Bambaataa and the Zulu Nation, Grandmaster Flash's innovations, Grand Wizard Theodore and scratching, beatboxing, the early recordings and MTV Raps, gangster rap and N.W.A, regional scenes (Southern, Dirty South, bounce), graffiti origins with TAKI 183 and Hugo, breakdancing history, the moonwalk, and fashion from Run-DMC to bling. The episode closes with listener mail from France and Israel.

segments.title: Selects intro and show opening
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Selects pick, How Hip Hop Works from July 2013, and the hosts open with banter about DJs and old-school hip hop.

segments.title: Hip hop vs. rap and the origin of the term
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish hip hop as a broader cultural movement from rap, a music style within it. They discuss who coined the term hip hop, with the Village Voice cited as an early print use.
topics: origin of the term hip hop

segments.title: The four pillars of hip hop culture
segments.summary: A cultural historian's four aspects of hip hop are listed: DJing, MCing/rapping, graffiti, and breakdancing/dance, along with broader visual arts, spoken word, and fashion style.

segments.title: African roots: griots and the slave ships
segments.summary: The hosts trace hip hop's roots to African oral storytelling traditions called griot, carried to the West Indies on slave ships, with drums, dance, and rhythm, plus church, gospel, jazz, and blues influences.

segments.title: Jamaican sound systems, toasting, and dub
segments.summary: After World War II, American soldiers in Jamaica carried musical influences back; Jamaican DJs with portable sound systems began toasting over records, which led to talkover and dub reggae.

segments.title: Clive Campbell and DJ Kool Herc's Bronx block parties
segments.summary: Clive Campbell moved from Jamaica to the Bronx in 1967 and became DJ Kool Herc, widely regarded as hip hop's originator. He started the break beat technique at parties, and his toasting led to early rapping.

segments.title: Afrika Bambaataa, Grandmaster Flash, and scratching
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Afrika Bambaataa and the Zulu Nation, Grandmaster Flash's electronics innovations such as the crossfader, punch phrasing, Grand Wizard Theodore's scratching origin story, and beatboxing.

segments.title: Early recordings, radio, and the rise of MCs
segments.summary: Hip hop moves from parties to recordings and radio, with Mr. Magic's Rap Attack as an early New York show. MCs become the frontmen, illustrated by DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince, and the Sugar Hill Gang's Rapper's Delight is cited as the first hit.
topics: DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince

segments.title: 1980s crossover, MTV, and gangster rap
segments.summary: Hip hop crosses over through Blondie's Rapture, Run-DMC, and others, and MTV Raps helps break down genre walls. Gangster rap, led by N.W.A and Ice-T, takes over and shifts the subject matter from the original positivity.

segments.title: Conscious rap, regional scenes, and modern trends
segments.summary: The hosts discuss groups like A Tribe Called Quest, De La Soul, Wu-Tang Clan, and Gang Starr, plus Southern scenes (2 Live Crew, Outcast, Goodie Mob) and the New Orleans bounce, and note later trends like Kanye West and Drake.

segments.title: Graffiti origins and the history of tagging
segments.summary: Graffiti is discussed as a related pillar of hip hop. Tagging traces to TAKI 183 in the 1960s, the New York Times wrote about him in 1971, and Hugo (Hayes) is linked to hip hop album art.

segments.title: Breakdancing history, moonwalk, and fashion
segments.summary: Breakdancing's roots are traced to West African movement, the cakewalk, Lindy Hop, and martial arts. The moonwalk, James Brown's influence, and 1980s breakdance fads are noted. Fashion covers loose clothing, Run-DMC's look, gold chains, African-inspired clothing, baggy styles, and hip hop business ventures.

segments.title: Listener mail from France and Israel
segments.summary: A listener named Julie writes from Paris, and Daniel writes from Jerusalem about his bakery boss discovering the show on his iTunes library. Josh and Chuck respond.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with a call to contact the show and a pointer to the website.
